title: The Cost of Elimination
short: Gaussian elimination takes about 2n³/3 arithmetic operations and each triangular solve about n², so doubling n multiplies the work by about 8.
trouble: Students compute A⁻¹ to solve Ax = b. Elimination is cheaper and usually more accurate.

blocks.html: You can solve a system by reducing it to Gaussian Elimination and Echelon Form and back substituting. On a computer the question becomes: how much work is that? We count flops (floating-point operations): each addition, subtraction, multiplication or division counts as one.

Gaussian elimination on an $n \times n$ matrix takes about $\frac{2}{3}n^{3}$ flops; each triangular solve (forward or back substitution) takes about $n^{2}$. Doubling $n$ multiplies the elimination work by about $2^{3} = 8$.

At step $k$, each of the $n - k$ rows below the pivot gets a multiplier (one division) and then has $n - k$ entries updated, each with a multiply and a subtract: about $2(n - k)^{2}$ flops for the step. Adding up, $$\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}2(n - k)^{2} = 2\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}j^{2} \approx \frac{2}{3}n^{3}.$$ In back substitution, the row $i$ places from the bottom needs $i - 1$ multiplies, $i - 1$ subtracts and one divide: $\sum_{i=1}^{n}(2i - 1) = n^{2}$.

blocks.title: Scaling up
blocks.q: Elimination on a $1{,}000 \times 1{,}000$ system takes $0.5$ s. Estimate the time for $2{,}000 \times 2{,}000$ and for $10{,}000 \times 10{,}000$.
steps: Work grows like $n^{3}$. Doubling $n$: $2^{3} = 8$ times the work, about $4$ s.
Multiplying $n$ by 10: $10^{3} = 1000$ times, about $500$ s, over 8 minutes.

blocks.title: Back substitution exactly
blocks.q: Count the flops of back substitution for $n = 4$.
steps: Next rows: $3$, then $5$, then $7$ flops (each adds one multiply and one subtract).

blocks.title: Many right-hand sides
blocks.q: A program must solve $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ for 100 different $\mathbf{b}$, with $n = 1000$. Compare redoing elimination each time with factoring once.
steps: Factor once ($PA = LU$, about $\frac{2}{3}n^{3} \approx 6.7 \times 10^{8}$), then two triangular solves per $\mathbf{b}$ ($100 \times 2n^{2} = 2 \times 10^{8}$): about $8.7 \times 10^{8}$ in all.
About 77 times less work. This is why libraries separate "factor" from "solve".
blocks.a: factoring once is about 77 times cheaper

blocks.name: num-system

opts.task: Slide $n$ and the number of right-hand sides. Is forming $A^{-1}$ ever the cheapest choice?

blocks.cap: Operation counts, and times at a billion operations per second, for three ways to solve many systems with the same matrix.

blocks.html: The same counting shows why computing $A^{-1}$ is a poor way to solve: forming the inverse means solving with all $n$ columns of the identity, about $2n^{3}$ flops, three times the cost of one elimination, and the product $A^{-1}\mathbf{b}$ is usually less accurate than elimination with pivoting.

Computing $A^{-1}$ to solve $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$. Even with many right-hand sides, an $LU$ factorization reused for each $\mathbf{b}$ costs no more than $A^{-1}$ and gives better answers. Write $\mathbf{x} = A^{-1}\mathbf{b}$ on paper if you like; on a computer, solve.
